claims.text: Strength and deformation behavior in AlCoCrFeNiTi are governed by dynamic strain aging.
Dynamic strain aging arises from transient interactions between mobile dislocations and local chemical heterogeneities, including nanoscale precipitates.
At lower strain rates and moderate temperatures, dislocations have sufficient time to interact with local chemical fluctuations.
Longer interactions between dislocations and local chemical fluctuations enhance dislocation pinning and produce serrated flow.
At higher strain rates, dislocations bypass the local obstacles more readily.
The baseline AlCoCrFeNiTi microstructure has a homogeneous elemental distribution.
The baseline microstructure may contain pre-existing nanoscale features.
Local chemical heterogeneities or nanoscale precipitates act as dynamic dislocation-pinning sites.
At lower strain rates, transient precipitate structures have enough time to develop and interact with dislocations.
Dynamic strain aging at lower strain rates increases yield strength.
Insufficient interaction time at higher strain rates prevents transient barriers from developing.
Easier dislocation bypass at higher strain rates causes lower strength and more uniform plastic flow.
Low-strain-rate, moderate-temperature tests will show higher yield strength than the high-rate baseline.
Low-strain-rate, moderate-temperature tests will show serrated flow.
Dislocation arrest or pinning events will spatially correlate with local chemical heterogeneities.
High-strain-rate tests will show reduced yield strength and smoother flow curves.
Dynamic strain-aging effects are minimal at high strain rates and/or temperatures.
The proposed mechanism applies from strain rates of 10^-4 to 10^-1 s^-1 and from room temperature to 300°C when oxidation and other environmental effects are minimized.
Outside the specified strain-rate and temperature ranges, other deformation mechanisms may dominate.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis assigns enhanced interactions to moderate temperatures, whereas the baseline groups high temperatures with high strain rates as conditions where interactions are minimal. No temperature transition is specified, so the roles of moderate versus high temperature within the room-temperature-to-300°C range are internally ambiguous.

The initial state is described as having a homogeneous elemental distribution, while the proposed governing mediator requires local chemical heterogeneities. These descriptions could coexist at different length scales, but the relevant scale of homogeneity is not stated.
